en: Praise of Noble Tārā composed by Ācārya Candradāsa.
Homage to Tārā!
O You whose moon-like feet are kissed by the abundant movement of the cresting rays from the beautiful crown-jewel of the wheel of bliss,
and whose eyes of compassionate pity are turned askance even toward the world of moving and unmoving beings; [I bow to You].
O Goddess, I perform for you this practice of offering praise through words and respectful service. || 1 ||
When you are present, those plunderers of the forest— fierce in tearing open the temples of elephants with the hard tips of their claws, protected by the cloth-like masses of their profuse blood,
and formidable as they strike at the hollows of mountain slopes with the loud, mocking laughter of their thick manes— [are subdued].
The sharp [intellects] instantly become blunt in power, even more so than the dull-witted.
Distraught by the dark ichor trickling from their broad, soiled temples,
dancing with a playful grace amidst the dense clamor of swarms of bees that stumble about them,
and scattering the dust of their lovely pastes as it is struck by the wind from their flapping ears;
On your path, the elephants—equal to the great mountain ranges and cherished by you with their pure [trunks]—do not move. || 3 ||

Terrorizing the quarters with the rapid cries of "Hā! Hā! from the city women as they were struck by the mass of fire-tongues leaping up with impetuosity due to the gusts of wind, [the conflagration] cast a dense darkness by shaking off the thick dust of smoky fumes.
The fire, having repeatedly followed the course of your supreme policy, attains tranquility. || 4 ||

For a man who possesses even the slightest bit of the name "Tārā," the dense and impenetrable forest ahead— filled with difficult passages where the creepers form curved canopies as they sway— is instantly crossed.
[He is not troubled by] the blazing fire flickering from the terrible hissing of a multitude of expanded hoods.
Poison is destroyed when the serpent spreads forth its throbbing and vast sparks of fire. || 5 ||
With the bolt-like arms of great strength, made terrifying by the stainless clash of the sharp, harsh sword drawn by hands trembling from a momentary fit of anger;
with an exceedingly cruel disposition, skilled in shattering the nearby thickets of travelers setting out on their path.
O Blessed One, because of your power, even in the forest no thief approaches one who possesses devotion to you.
Even he who was once restrained by the seizing of the hair and the roar of the hero among kings,
now like one possessed by a planet, his skeletal frame shattered by the jingling of ropes;
with his rows of harsh iron chains making a clattering sound that resounds at every step—
Having prostrated before your lotus-like feet, he rejoices, freed from all bonds.

From the ocean— which was difficult to cross even with its violent mass of crocodiles due to its sharp claws, and whose vast, thick shores and *tāla* tree shoots were tossed by the winds of the dark fortnight as they played upon the waters of restless waves thick with tumultuous clamor— [he emerged] with impetuosity.
O Savior, you come to protect one who is distressed, with eyes as tremulous and wide as stars.

O Tāriṇī, who can take any form at will, those who bow to you are liberated from that moment by the onset of your great grace— [you] whose nostrils are filled with a terrible, gurgling sound produced by the intense heat of the vital essence of subtle, piercing cries, and whose feet and hands are smeared with blood dripping from the boiling carcasses of bodies.
At that moment, her circular cheeks were adorned with jeweled earrings whose shimmering rays were set in motion.
With his waist girdled by a tattered rag strewn with lice,
intent on filling his belly by scavenging for morsels of food from others,
if indeed that lone Rākṣasa should place your name upon his heart—
[He saw] a variegated chowrie, studded with gold, being waved by a mature woman.
The *Āryatārāstuti* composed by Śrī Candradāsa is completed.
